  tmux, short for “terminal multiplexer,” belongs to a long tradition of Unix tools built
  around one simple idea: a command-line session should survive beyond the life of a single
  terminal window. Before tmux existed, users relied heavily on GNU Screen, first released
  in the late 1980s. Screen allowed people to run multiple shell sessions inside one
  terminal, detach from them, and reconnect later. This was especially useful for system
  administrators working over unreliable SSH connections.

  tmux emerged in the late 2000s as a cleaner, more modern alternative. It was created by
  Nicholas Marriott and developed closely with the OpenBSD community. Like many OpenBSD
  projects, tmux emphasized simplicity, portability, security-conscious design, and a
  permissive license. Rather than merely copying Screen, tmux introduced a clearer client-
  server architecture: sessions run in the background, while terminal windows act as clients
  connecting to them.

  Its design made several workflows easier. Users could split terminal windows into panes,
  organize work into windows and sessions, detach from remote tasks, and later resume
  exactly where they left off. Developers, sysadmins, and power users quickly adopted it
  because it fit naturally into SSH-heavy environments, long-running build processes, log
  monitoring, and editor-based workflows.

  Over time, tmux gained a reputation for being more scriptable and configurable than
  Screen. Its command system made automation practical, while its status bar, key bindings,
  layouts, and hooks let users shape it into a personal workspace manager. On macOS, Linux,
  BSD systems, and remote servers, tmux became a standard part of many development
  environments.

  By the 2010s, tmux had become especially popular among programmers using Vim, Emacs, and
  terminal-based tools. Blog posts, dotfile repositories, and tutorials spread common
  configurations. Plugins and plugin managers appeared, adding session restoration, sensible
  defaults, theming, and integration with editors.

  The history of tmux is not one of flashy reinvention, but of careful refinement. It solved
  an old Unix problem with modern taste: keep work alive, organized, and reachable. Its
  success comes from being boring in the best sense: reliable, scriptable, portable, and
  respectful of how command-line users actually work. Today, tmux remains one of the
  essential tools for anyone who spends serious time in a terminal.
